# Digital sleep-coaching versus sleep hygiene leaflet in adults with insomnia: a randomized trial

> FIXTURE (self-test): synthetic material created for pipeline self-testing. Numbers are internally consistent but this is NOT a real publication and must not be cited as evidence.

## Abstract

We report a two-arm randomized controlled trial comparing a 6-week digital sleep-coaching program with a standard sleep-hygiene leaflet in adults with chronic insomnia. Four hundred twelve participants were randomized 1:1. The primary endpoint was change in Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) at week 6. The coaching arm improved by 4.8 points more than the leaflet arm (95% CI 3.5 to 6.1, p < 0.001). Intervention adherence, defined as completion of at least 80% of scheduled sessions, was 78.2% in the coaching arm and 41.5% in the leaflet arm. No serious adverse events were attributed to the intervention.

## 1 Introduction

Chronic insomnia affects roughly one in ten adults and is a first-line target for digital interventions because cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is resource-limited. Prior trials of self-guided digital CBT-I report smaller effects than therapist-delivered care, and it remains unclear whether light-touch coaching (asynchronous feedback) preserves efficacy. The present trial asks whether adding brief asynchronous coaching to a digital CBT-I program produces a clinically meaningful ISI improvement compared with a leaflet-only control.

## 2 Methods

### 2.1 Design and participants

Parallel-group, single-blind (assessor-blinded) randomized trial at three community sites. Eligibility: adults aged 18-65 with ISI >= 15 and insomnia duration >= 3 months. Exclusion: apnea (AHI > 15), night-shift work, current CBT-I.

### 2.2 Randomization and intervention

Participants were randomized 1:1 using block randomization (block size 8) stratified by site and baseline ISI (>= 22 versus < 22). The intervention comprised six weekly modules plus asynchronous coach messages within 24 hours of module completion. The control condition was a 12-page sleep-hygiene leaflet with no reminders.

### 2.3 Outcomes and analysis

Primary outcome: ISI change from baseline to week 6. Secondary outcomes: sleep-onset latency (SOL), wake after sleep onset (WASO), and sleep efficiency (SE) from 7-day actigraphy. Analysis used intention-to-treat with multiple imputation (20 imputations); between-arm differences are reported with 95% confidence intervals. The trial was powered for a 3.0-point ISI difference (alpha 0.05, power 0.90), requiring 196 per arm.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Primary outcome

![Figure 1. Actigraphy sleep efficiency by study week for the coaching and leaflet arms](figures/fig1.png)

Baseline ISI was 19.6 (SD 3.1) in the coaching arm and 19.4 (SD 3.0) in the leaflet arm. At week 6, ISI decreased by 8.1 points (SD 5.2) with coaching and by 3.3 points (SD 5.6) with the leaflet, a between-arm difference of 4.8 points (95% CI 3.5 to 6.1, p < 0.001, Cohen d = 0.89). Remission (ISI < 8) was reached by 46.6% of the coaching arm versus 24.3% of the leaflet arm (risk difference 22.3 percentage points, 95% CI 13.1 to 31.2).

### 3.2 Secondary outcomes and adherence

Actigraphy showed SE gains of 6.4 percentage points with coaching versus 1.9 with the leaflet (difference 4.5, 95% CI 2.6 to 6.4). SOL fell by 14.2 minutes with coaching and 5.1 minutes with the leaflet. Adherence to at least 80% of modules was 78.2% in the coaching arm and 41.5% in the leaflet arm (p < 0.001). Median time to first coach reply was 7.3 hours (IQR 4.1 to 15.6).

### 3.3 Safety and attrition

Retention at week 6 was 91.7% (coaching) and 89.3% (leaflet); the difference was not significant (p = 0.38). Two participants in the coaching arm reported transient worsening of sleep that resolved without withdrawal; no serious adverse events were intervention-related.

## 4 Discussion

The observed difference exceeds the 3.0-point threshold used for sample-size planning and is consistent with a clinically meaningful benefit of asynchronous coaching over leaflet-only care. Because the control condition received written instructions but no reminders, part of the effect may reflect engagement rather than CBT-I content per se.

## 5 Limitations

First, participants and coaches were not blinded, so expectancy effects cannot be excluded; assessors were blinded but self-reported ISI remains subjective. Second, follow-up ended at week 6, so durability beyond the intervention window is unknown. Third, adherence was self-recorded in the app, which may overstate completion relative to server-side logs. Fourth, the sample was recruited from three community sites in one country, limiting generalizability to clinical populations with psychiatric comorbidity. Fifth, actigraphy underestimates wakefulness in participants with low sleep efficiency.
